verdicts.strongest_argument: The datapoint is published, on the hunter's own URL, five days before the print, in JCK — the jewelry industry's primary trade publication — and it is not a one-off leak but the September instalment of a monthly public series: Edge Retail Academy posts it on its own blog and JCK/InStore carried the June (+18%) and July (+10%) readings the same way, so the deceleration path the finding draws is itself a published series rather than a discovered one. Two further discounts. First, the macro narrative it embodies is exactly the stated cause of the 13.15% one-month drawdown already in the tape: Zacks/Yahoo and TipRanks catalyst pieces in the past month attribute SIG's slide to 'weak consumer demand and high gold prices squeezing profitability' and 'worries about a broader slowdown in middle-market jewelry buying' — which is verbatim the units-down / average-ticket-up shape of the Edge panel, and the World Gold Council's Q2 2026 release already put global jewellery volume at its lowest quarterly tonnage since the pandemic. Second, the panel is a poor proxy for Signet. Edge aggregates thousands of independent fine-jewelry stores, which skew natural-diamond bridal, custom and higher-ticket; Signet is mall and off-mall chain (Kay/Zales/Jared) plus Blue Nile/James Allen digital, is over 45% lab-grown in engagement rings, and has been running comps that diverge from the independent channel (Kay/Zales/Jared +6% comp in FY26 Q3). And August is fiscal Q3 month one — Signet's Q2 ended ~2026-08-01 — so it cannot touch a single reported number tomorrow. It reaches the print only through the Q3 comp guide, which is a real channel (UBS is publicly looking for low-single-digit positive Q3 comp guidance) but an indirect one. Against that, I concede what is genuinely undrawn: no equity-side coverage I could find connects the August Edge print to Signet's Q3 guide, and the stock did not move on 2026-09-03 (close 81.26 on 09-01, spot 82.06 on 09-08). That undrawn connection is why this is mid-scale and not 80.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Edge Retail Academy August 2026: gross sales +5%, units -8%, average retail sale +14%; sterling silver and alternative metals -5% dollars, -19% units.

The July instalment of the same Edge series: +10% gross, units -2%, average retail sale +12%, explicitly noting June was +18% with flat units — i.e. the deceleration path was already public a month ago.
The June instalment (+18% gross, stronger unit performance), establishing the monthly cadence of this release.
Attributes SIG's slide to weak discretionary demand, high gold prices and worries about a slowdown in middle-market jewelry buying — the same thesis as the Edge panel.
Q2 2026 global jewellery demand fell to 278t, the lowest quarterly volume since the pandemic, on high gold prices — the units-down / value-up mechanism, already public.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The 20-day run-up of -13.15% is the tape already expressing this exact narrative; contemporaneous wire copy names weak jewelry demand and gold-driven margin pressure as the cause. Crucially, the drawdown was essentially complete before the Edge August print: SIG closed 81.26 on 2026-09-01, and spot is 82.06 on 2026-09-08, so the 09-03 publication produced no move. The -13.46 skew (calls bid) points the other way, but I would not lean on it — total front-expiry OI is 1,777 contracts, the ATM spread is 65% of mid, and the put/call OI ratio is 3.27, so the skew here is close to noise.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that Signet's own comps track the Edge independent panel with a usable correlation, or a Signet-specific August channel check (mall traffic, Kay/Zales web pricing) showing the same -8% unit shape, would move this well below 40.

verdicts.strongest_argument: I refute this one on the facts before reaching the price. Two errors, and they invert the sign. (1) The Section 122 surcharge was 10% ad valorem, not 15%. The White House proclamation of 2026-02-20 says so in terms — 'I impose, for a period of 150 days, a temporary import surcharge of 10 percent ad valorem ... effective February 24, 2026' — and Gibson Dunn was still describing 'the current 10-percent-Section-122 tariffs' in its May 2026 CIT alert, while GHY's trade-compliance update (published 02-21, updated 02-24) states flatly that 'there have been no official communications supporting the 15% duty rate.' 15% is the statutory ceiling of Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, not the rate imposed; Global Trade Alert is the only source I found modelling 15%, and it is an outlier against the proclamation text. (2) India's Section 301 forced-labor rate is 10%, per Honigman's own alert and per National Jeweler's trade coverage on 2026-07-24, which characterises the new 10–12.5% band against the prior across-the-board 10% as 'either maintenance or an increase.' So the transition for India is 10% to 10% — flat, not a 2.5–5 point step down. Across Signet's wider sourcing base it is worse than flat: China goes from 10%+25% to 12.5%+25%, and Thailand, Vietnam and the UAE all land in the 12.5% tier. There is no tariff tailwind here of the shape claimed. Separately, and independent of the arithmetic: the event is in the wire copy. Honigman, National Jeweler and Centurion Jewelry all covered it on or about 2026-07-24, 45 days before the print, and Centurion's piece is specifically headlined on jewelry-sourcing countries and notes Signet's heavy India sourcing; Simply Wall St has published Signet-specific tariff-exposure valuation notes quantifying the India dependence ('sources roughly half its merchandise from India'). Finally the mechanism barely reaches Q2 at all — 2026-07-24 leaves roughly one week inside a quarter that ended ~08-01, against months of inventory already landed, so it is a guide item only, and a guide raise on tariff relief is precisely what UBS published on 2026-09-08 (35–40 cents on the low end) and what the market is already looking for. The one real change the finding does not make — Section 301 exempts precious metals in raw and semi-manufactured form across all 60 economies — is also public in National Jeweler's 07-24 piece.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Sets the Section 122 surcharge at 10 percent ad valorem for 150 days effective 2026-02-24 — refuting the finding's '15%' premise at the primary source.
Confirms 10% in effect from 02-24 and states there were no official communications supporting a 15% rate.
Refers throughout to 'the current 10-percent-Section-122 tariffs' as of May 2026, after the alleged 15% amendment would have taken effect.

Jewelry-trade coverage of the same transition: prior measure was a temporary 10% across-the-board tariff, India lands at 10% under Section 301, so the new 10–12.5% band is maintenance or an increase, not a cut; also notes the raw/semi-manufactured precious-metals exemption.
Jewelry-trade piece specifically on the Section 301 rates across major jewelry-sourcing countries, naming Signet's significant India sourcing; India 10%, China/Thailand/Vietnam/UAE 12.5%.
The hunter's own source: India in the 10% additive tier, China 12.5% on top of the existing 25% for 37.5% — i.e. no India step down and a China step up.

Published preview: UBS's Serna expects Signet to lift the low end of FY27 EPS guidance by 35–40 cents and guide Q3 comps positive low-single-digit — the guide raise this finding's mechanism would produce is already the published expectation.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The 25-delta skew of -13.46 (calls bid over puts) and the published 2026-09-08 UBS-driven preview both say the market is already paying for a guidance raise, which is the only channel through which a 2026-07-24 tariff change could reach this print. Caveat honestly: with 1,777 total OI and a 65%-of-mid ATM spread, the skew is thin enough that I rest this on the published preview rather than on the options. The tape shows no bounce around 07-24 — SIG is -13.15% over twenty days — which is consistent with there being no tailwind to price.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A CBP CSMS message or Federal Register notice showing the Section 122 surcharge was in fact collected at 15% through 2026-07-23 would restore the arithmetic and drop this to roughly 55 on publication grounds alone.

verdicts.strongest_argument: The fact is in the most public place a company fact can be: Signet's own Q1 FY27 earnings call on 2026-06-02, which is the hunter's own URL, and the accompanying 10-Q. Management volunteered it unprompted, and their exact words also cap the size and correct the finding: they are 'the importer of record on a small fraction of our purchases,' they have 'already submitted claims for most of those purchases,' and — contra the finding's 'the FY27 guide contains none of it' — the guidance explicitly includes a 'minimal tariff refund benefit.' So it is not excluded, it is included at a small number, and the reason it is small is structural: the bulk of Signet's merchandise arrives DDP through vendors, so those IEEPA refunds accrue to the vendors, not to Signet. Sizing it against Signet's own numbers: on roughly $3.0–3.5bn of annual merchandise purchases, a 'small fraction' as importer of record over the ~11 months IEEPA duties were collected, at a low-to-mid-teens effective rate, is order-of-magnitude $30–50m pre-tax plus statutory interest, on ~39.5m shares — real but a one-time, low-multiple item against $480–560m of adjusted operating income, and one the market will likely back out of adjusted EPS. The CBP scaffolding is accurate and public: the ~82% coverage figure comes from CBP's own status report to the CIT dated 2026-04-09 and was carried by Thompson Hine on 2026-04, and the CAPE launch on 2026-04-20 with 60–90 day turnaround was covered by NRF, RSM, Norton Rose Fulbright, UPS and National Jeweler — none of it Signet-specific. Simply Wall St has also published Signet-specific pieces on the tariff ruling reshaping its cost outlook. What I concede: I could find no analyst or press item that sizes Signet's refund, and none that draws the specific timing link — CBP mass-refunding through Signet's Q2, therefore a quantification or a P&L credit is plausible tomorrow. That undrawn timing link, plus the genuine possibility management uses the call to put a number on it for the first time, is what keeps this from 80. It is the one of the three that has a live, in-window channel to the print.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Management discloses on the record that Signet is importer of record on a small fraction of purchases, has filed claims for most of them, has received a small amount, cannot yet quantify amount or timing, and that guidance includes a minimal tariff refund benefit.
CBP's status report to the CIT: as of 2026-04-09, 56,000+ importers of record registered, covering ~82% of entries and ~$127bn in IEEPA duties eligible for electronic refund.
CAPE launched 2026-04-20; refunds generally issued 60–90 days after acceptance; over $160bn of IEEPA duties at stake.
Jewelry-trade explainer on the refund portal and process, i.e. the mechanism is public within Signet's own sector press.

CBP's own page confirms Phase 1 scope is limited to certain unliquidated entries and entries within 80 days of liquidation, with later phases unannounced — a brake on the 'refunds all land now' framing.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Calls bid over puts (-13.46 skew) and a published 2026-09-08 preview looking for a 35–40 cent low-end guidance raise are consistent with the market already expecting a positive revision from tariff-related relief, of which refunds are one component; but with 1,777 contracts of OI and a 65%-of-mid ATM spread I treat the skew as weak corroboration only. No identifiable move in the tape on 2026-04-20 (CAPE launch) or 2026-06-02 attributable to refunds — the 06-02 print moved +3.75% on the quarter as a whole.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: If Signet's Q1 FY27 10-Q disclosed a refund receivable large enough to be quantified, or if a sell-side note has already sized it, this goes to 85; if the company has never disclosed its importer-of-record share and tomorrow is the first quantification, it drops toward 40.

interactions: SIG#1 and SIG#2 are not two independent positives. Both rest on the same document — the 2026-06-02 Q1 FY27 transcript, where the 'mid-teens effective tariff rate for the year' and the IEEPA refund language sit in adjacent passages — and both resolve through the same single channel, an upward revision to the FY27 guide on tariff relief. That is one bet, not two, and it is the bet already published on 2026-09-08 (UBS: lift the low end 35–40 cents) and the one the -13.46 skew is nominally paying for, so they should not be additively scored. They also share the same weakness: neither has a Q2 P&L channel worth much, because SIG#1 lands one week before quarter-end against months of landed inventory and SIG#2 is capped by management's own 'small fraction of our purchases.' SIG#0 is the direct mirror of both: it argues the Q3 comp guide disappoints the low-single-digit-positive expectation, while SIG#1 and SIG#2 argue the FY EPS guide gets raised — and both can be true at once (better gross margin on tariffs, softer top line on gold-inflated tickets and falling units), which is the most likely combination and roughly the shape already in the price. Note also that SIG#0 and SIG#1 share an unexamined common driver in the gold price: the +14% average retail sale in the Edge panel and the commodity-driven merchandise margin pressure in Signet's own guide are the same phenomenon, and neither finding is about tariffs or demand in isolation.
